flu-or-cold-how-they-differ.name: Flu or a cold: how they differ
flu-or-cold-how-they-differ.headline: Flu or a cold: how to tell them apart, how long each lasts and when to get help
flu-or-cold-how-they-differ.summary: Flu tends to start faster and feel worse than a cold, with fever, aches and exhaustion; a cold mostly stays in the nose and throat.
keyPoints: Cold and flu symptoms overlap, but flu tends to be more severe and often comes on within hours.
A cold mainly affects the nose and throat and builds up gradually.
Antibiotics do not work against colds or flu, because both are caused by viruses.
Sudden chest pain, severe breathlessness or coughing up blood needs 999 or A&E.
NHS 111 or a GP can advise if symptoms get worse or last longer than expected.

body.heading: How do flu and a cold differ?
body.body:
Colds and flu are both viral infections that affect the nose and throat, and their symptoms overlap. Flu and colds differ in how severe they are and in how quickly they start.

Flu tends to be more severe than a cold. A cold mostly affects the nose and throat, while flu can also bring a fever, aches and exhaustion.

Because the symptoms overlap, it can be hard to tell flu and a cold apart from symptoms alone. With a cold a person usually feels unwell but can manage usual activities, while flu can leave a person exhausted and too unwell to carry on as normal.

body.heading: How quickly do the symptoms start?
body.body:
Speed of onset is another difference the NHS pages point to. Flu tends to come on suddenly, often within hours.

A cold usually builds more gradually. The main signs of a cold are a blocked or runny nose, sneezing, a sore throat, a hoarse voice, a cough, and feeling tired and unwell.

body.heading: How long do they last?
body.body:
Most people start to feel better from a cold within about one to two weeks. Flu usually improves within about a week.

Tiredness can linger for longer after flu, even when the other symptoms have settled.

body.heading: What treatment is there?
body.body:
A cold is caused by a virus and usually gets better by itself. The NHS says the usual approach is to rest and drink fluids while the body clears the infection.

For a cold, a pharmacist can recommend suitable medicines and check which ones are suitable for the person. Antibiotics do not help, because both illnesses are caused by viruses rather than bacteria.

A flu vaccine protects against flu, but it does not protect against colds.

A pharmacist can recommend suitable cold medicines and check which ones are suitable for the person, and some are not suitable for children, pregnant women or people taking certain other medicines.

body.heading: When should someone get medical help?
body.body:
The NHS separates emergencies from problems that can wait for a call or an appointment.

Sudden chest pain, severe difficulty breathing or coughing up blood is an emergency, and the route is 999 or A&E.

For less urgent worries, NHS 111 or the GP can advise. The NHS says to get an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 for flu symptoms with feeling very unwell, shortness of breath or no improvement.

The NHS says people aged 65 or over, people who are pregnant, and people with a long-term condition or a weakened immune system should get an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 if they have flu symptoms.

The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden chest pain, severe difficulty breathing or coughing up blood, with someone else driving or an ambulance rather than the person driving themselves.

body.heading: Is it flu, a cold or something else?
body.body:
Other infections can look like flu or a cold. The UKHSA publishes a guide to the signs and symptoms of flu, COVID-19 and colds, and the NHS pages for each illness set out what to look for.

Symptoms overlap, so the only way to know for sure whether a person has flu or COVID-19 is a test.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: Flu symptoms can include a sudden high temperature, an aching body and feeling exhausted. A cold usually causes a runny or blocked nose, sneezing, watery eyes and a sore throat, and does not usually bring a fever or body aches. The NHS offers the flu vaccine every year, in autumn or winter, to people at higher risk of becoming seriously ill from flu.

references.title: UKHSA: Do I have flu, COVID-19 or a cold? Know the signs and symptoms

type-1-and-type-2-diabetes-compared.name: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes compared
type-1-and-type-2-diabetes-compared.headline: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes compared: causes, symptoms and treatment
type-1-and-type-2-diabetes-compared.summary: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition treated with insulin; type 2 develops when the body makes too little insulin or it works poorly.
keyPoints: In type 1 diabetes the immune system attacks and destroys the cells that make insulin.
In type 2 diabetes the body makes too little insulin or the insulin it makes does not work well.
Type 1 often develops quickly, especially in young people, while type 2 develops slowly over years.
Type 1 is treated with insulin and blood glucose checks; type 2 is managed with lifestyle changes and sometimes medicines.
There is no cure for diabetes at the moment, although type 2 can sometimes go into remission.

body.heading: What do the two types have in common?
body.body:
Diabetes is a condition in which there is too much glucose, a type of sugar, in the blood. Both type 1 and type 2 involve insulin, a hormone made by cells in the pancreas.

The two types share several symptoms: increased thirst, passing urine more often, tiredness and weight loss. The difference lies in why the problem arises and how it is managed.

body.heading: What causes type 1 diabetes?
body.body:
Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition. The immune system attacks and destroys the cells in the pancreas that make insulin.

In young people the symptoms usually develop very quickly, over a few days or weeks. In adults, the symptoms often take longer to develop, sometimes a few months.

body.heading: What causes type 2 diabetes?
body.body:
Either the body does not make enough insulin, or the insulin it makes does not work as well as it should.

Diabetes UK lists age, family history, ethnicity and weight among the risk factors.

Type 2 develops slowly over a period of years, so the signs may not be obvious.

body.heading: How are the two types treated?
body.body:
Type 1 diabetes is treated with insulin, which is needed for life, alongside monitoring of blood glucose.

Type 2 diabetes is managed with lifestyle changes such as eating healthily, exercising and trying to lose weight, and sometimes with medicines. Medicine may be added if needed, such as metformin, and some people also need insulin.

body.heading: Can diabetes be cured?
body.body:
Diabetes UK says there is no cure for diabetes at the moment. Type 2 diabetes can sometimes be put into remission, and it can sometimes be prevented.

Remission does not mean the condition has gone for good, which is why regular checks are still part of care.

body.heading: How is diabetes checked, and who should be seen?
body.body:
Blood tests are used to diagnose and monitor diabetes. The site's pages on blood glucose and on HbA1c explain what they show, and the laboratory report shows the reference range used.

The NHS says to get a GP appointment as soon as possible for the main symptoms of diabetes; for a child, to contact the GP practice urgently or use NHS 111 if unsure what to do. The NHS website sets out the symptoms to look for.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: For a child with diabetes symptoms, contact the GP practice urgently or use NHS 111 if unsure; call 999 if a child is very drowsy, confused, breathing fast or deeply, has severe tummy pain or keeps vomiting. In someone with diabetes, loss of appetite, feeling or being sick, a high temperature, stomach pain or fruity-smelling breath needs urgent medical attention, so call NHS 111 or 999 if severe. Remission means blood sugar stays below the diabetes level for at least six months without diabetes medicine.

references.title: Diabetes UK: Differences between type 1 and type 2 diabetes

heart-attack-cardiac-arrest-and-angina.name: Heart attack, cardiac arrest and angina
heart-attack-cardiac-arrest-and-angina.headline: Heart attack, cardiac arrest and angina: the differences and when to call 999
heart-attack-cardiac-arrest-and-angina.summary: A heart attack is a blocked blood supply to the heart muscle, cardiac arrest is the heart stopping, and angina is chest pain that eases with rest.
keyPoints: A heart attack happens when the blood flow to the heart is blocked.
In a cardiac arrest the heart stops pumping effectively, the person collapses and is not breathing normally.
Angina is chest pain caused by a temporary reduction in the blood supply to the heart.
Angina symptoms usually ease with rest or a nitrate medicine, whereas heart attack symptoms usually do not.
For a suspected heart attack or cardiac arrest the NHS says to call 999 straight away.

body.heading: What is the difference between a heart attack and cardiac arrest?
body.body:
The British Heart Foundation (BHF) explains that a heart attack and a cardiac arrest are different, and that both are emergencies.

A heart attack happens when the blood flow to the heart is blocked. The BHF describes a heart attack as a sudden loss of blood flow to part of the heart muscle, and the NHS says it can be life-threatening and needs emergency treatment in hospital.

In a cardiac arrest the heart stops pumping effectively. The person collapses, does not respond and is not breathing normally. The BHF says a heart attack can sometimes lead to a cardiac arrest.

If a defibrillator is nearby, the 999 call handler will say where it is and may ask someone to fetch it, and CPR should not be stopped.

A cardiac arrest usually happens suddenly and without warning.

body.heading: What is angina?
body.body:
Angina is chest pain or discomfort that happens when the blood supply to the heart muscle is temporarily reduced. The BHF says the discomfort of angina does not damage the heart muscle in the way a heart attack does.

Angina symptoms usually happen during exercise and pass within a few minutes, and they can be eased by resting or by using a nitrate tablet or spray.

Angina symptoms usually pass in a few minutes, but heart pain that lasts longer may be a heart attack, so call 999.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of a heart attack?
body.body:
The NHS lists chest pain that feels tight or squeezing. The pain can spread to the arms, jaw, neck, back or tummy.

Other signs include feeling sick, sweating, shortness of breath and light-headedness.

A key difference from angina is that heart attack symptoms are not usually relieved by a nitrate tablet or spray.

Some people with a heart attack also look pale or grey.

Women are more likely to notice symptoms such as shortness of breath, feeling sick, and back or jaw pain, and symptoms can be milder than people expect.

body.heading: What are the signs of a cardiac arrest?
body.body:
A person in cardiac arrest loses consciousness. They do not respond, and they are not breathing or their breathing does not look normal.

Without treatment a person in cardiac arrest may die within minutes, which is why speed matters.

body.heading: When should someone call 999?
body.body:
The NHS says to call 999 straight away if someone may be having a heart attack.

If someone seems to be in cardiac arrest, the NHS advises calling 999 and starting CPR, with the call handler giving instructions.

The NHS says to call 999 for the main warning signs of a heart attack, and to call NHS 111 for less severe symptoms such as a racing or irregular heartbeat. The BHF says heart attack pain is not relieved by rest or a nitrate medicine, and that a heart attack is a 999 emergency.

The NHS advises a person who may be having a heart attack to call 999 rather than drive themselves to A&E.

For less severe symptoms such as a racing or irregular heartbeat, the NHS says to call NHS 111.

body.heading: How are they diagnosed and treated?
body.body:
A heart attack is usually assessed with an ECG, which records the heart's electrical activity, and a blood test for troponin, a protein released when the heart muscle is damaged. The site's pages on these tests give more detail.

Treatment in hospital, with medicine or a procedure, aims to restore the blood supply to the heart.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: An NHS ECG is usually the first test, and it can show whether the heart attack needs urgent treatment to open the blocked artery.

references.title: NHS: Symptoms of a heart attack
British Heart Foundation: Cardiac arrest vs heart attack, what's the difference?

stroke-and-tia-spotting-the-signs.name: Stroke and TIA: spotting the signs
stroke-and-tia-spotting-the-signs.headline: Stroke and TIA: spotting the signs and why 999 is the route
stroke-and-tia-spotting-the-signs.summary: A stroke and a TIA are both emergencies: the NHS and the Stroke Association say to call 999 even if the symptoms pass.
keyPoints: The FAST test checks for face drooping, arm weakness and speech problems, and the NHS says to call 999 if any sign is present.
A TIA, sometimes called a mini-stroke, is a temporary disruption of the blood supply to the brain, and its symptoms recover completely within 24 hours.
Symptoms of a TIA can pass, but the person still needs to be assessed in hospital, so call 999.
Treatment differs for strokes caused by a blood clot and strokes caused by bleeding, which is why a hospital scan comes first.
The Stroke Association runs a support helpline for people affected by stroke.

body.heading: What are the signs of a stroke?
body.body:
The FAST test is used across the UK to spot a stroke. It checks the face, the arms and the speech: has the mouth or eye drooped, can the person raise both arms fully and keep them there, and is their speech slurred or hard to understand.

The NHS and the Stroke Association say that any one of these signs is a reason to call 999. NHS England has found that many people wait too long to call 999, with an average of 88 minutes between the first symptom and the call.

If any one of these signs is seen, the NHS says to call 999. It also says not to wait for more symptoms to appear.

A stroke is a medical emergency, so call 999 even if symptoms seem minor or go away.

body.heading: What is a TIA, and how does it differ from a stroke?
body.body:
A transient ischaemic attack, or TIA, is often called a mini-stroke. A TIA is a temporary disruption of the blood supply to part of the brain.

NHS hospital guidance says the symptoms of a TIA recover completely within 24 hours. If symptoms last longer than that, it is classed as a stroke.

The NHS and the Stroke Association say to call 999 for a suspected stroke or TIA, even if the symptoms seem minor or go away.

A TIA is a temporary disruption of the blood supply to part of the brain.

body.heading: Why does a TIA matter if the symptoms pass?
body.body:
After a suspected TIA there is a risk of a stroke, which is why aspirin is given straight away to help prevent one.

For this reason the NHS says a suspected TIA should be assessed urgently, even if the symptoms have gone by the time the ambulance arrives. A person whose symptoms have cleared still needs to be seen in hospital.

body.heading: What happens in hospital?
body.body:
A scan is used to find out whether a stroke is caused by a blood clot (ischaemic) or by bleeding in the brain (haemorrhagic), because the treatments differ.

For an ischaemic stroke, emergency options include clot-busting medicine, called thrombolysis, and removal of the clot with a catheter, called thrombectomy. A stroke caused by bleeding is treated differently, with treatment aimed at stopping the bleeding and relieving pressure on the brain, sometimes with surgery.

Hospital teams aim to scan the brain soon after symptoms begin, which is part of why calling 999 matters.

A brain scan is done soon after symptoms begin to show whether a stroke is caused by a clot or a bleed.

Clot-busting drugs carry a risk of bleeding, so doctors weigh the risk against the benefit for each person.

Thrombectomy is used for clots that are too large for clot-busting drugs to break down.

body.heading: How is a suspected TIA treated?
body.body:
For a suspected TIA, the NHS says aspirin is usually given to lower the risk of a stroke, unless there is a medical reason to avoid it. The NHS says the person should be referred to a specialist within 24 hours of the start of their symptoms.

Care after a TIA can include a blood thinner such as aspirin, a statin, and blood pressure tablets if needed. Medicines that thin the blood or reduce clotting may be used, and sometimes surgery is offered to clear a narrowed artery in the neck.

After a TIA, treatment can include a blood thinner, a statin and blood pressure tablets if needed, and some people have surgery to unblock a narrowed neck artery.

body.heading: Where can people find support?
body.body:
The Stroke Association runs a Stroke Helpline on 0303 3033 100 for stroke survivors, their families and carers.

A GP can explain what the diagnosis means and arrange follow-up care. In an emergency, the route is always 999.

The Stroke Association helpline is free to use and supports stroke survivors, families and carers.

references.title: Stroke Association: Stroke signs and symptoms
Stroke Association: TIA diagnosis and treatment

asthma-and-copd-how-they-differ.name: Asthma and COPD: how they differ
asthma-and-copd-how-they-differ.headline: Asthma and COPD: how they differ in cause, symptoms and treatment
asthma-and-copd-how-they-differ.summary: Asthma is a long-term airway condition whose symptoms come and go; COPD is mostly smoking-related and tends to get worse over time.
keyPoints: Asthma symptoms can come and go, while COPD symptoms usually get progressively worse without treatment.
The main cause of COPD is smoking, though it can affect people who have never smoked.
Clinicians use a person's history, an examination and breathing tests such as spirometry to tell the two apart.
Asthma is mainly treated with inhalers; COPD has no cure, but treatment and stopping smoking can help slow it.
In an asthma attack, the NHS says to call 999 if a person does not feel better after using the reliever inhaler as directed, or feels worse at any time.

body.heading: What is asthma?
body.body:
Asthma is a long-term condition that affects the airways. The NHS says the main symptoms are wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath and a tight chest, and that they often come and go.

Common triggers include exercise, cold air, air pollution and allergens such as pollen or dust. The NHS says the exact cause of asthma is not fully understood, but allergies, a family history of asthma or allergies, and early-life exposure to air pollution or cigarette smoke are among the factors linked with it.

During an asthma attack, sitting up and staying calm is part of the usual NHS advice while using the reliever inhaler as directed, and 999 should be called if there is no improvement.

body.heading: What is COPD?
body.body:
COPD, short for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, is the name for a group of lung conditions that cause breathing difficulties. It includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis.

The NHS says the main cause is smoking, although it can sometimes affect people who have never smoked. Typical symptoms are breathlessness on exertion, a persistent chesty cough with phlegm, frequent chest infections and wheeze. They tend to get worse over time.

With COPD there can also be periods when symptoms suddenly get worse, known as a flare-up.

body.heading: How do doctors tell them apart?
body.body:
NICE says that when someone first presents with symptoms, untreated COPD and asthma can frequently be told apart from the person's history and an examination. NICE advises using features from the person's history and examination to help tell the two conditions apart.

Breathing tests help. Spirometry is a breathing test that supports a diagnosis of COPD, and lung function tests also form part of diagnosing asthma, although a normal result does not always rule asthma out. The site's spirometry page explains the test.

Because symptoms vary and breathing problems have more than one cause, the NHS notes that diagnosing asthma can take time.

body.heading: How are the two treated?
body.body:
The NHS says inhalers are the main treatment for asthma. Reliever inhalers ease symptoms when they occur, and preventer inhalers are used regularly to reduce them. An asthma action plan is usually agreed with a doctor or asthma nurse.

There is currently no cure for COPD, but treatment can help slow its progression and control symptoms, and for people who smoke, stopping smoking is the most important step. Treatment mainly relieves symptoms, with inhalers, and pulmonary rehabilitation may help people become more active.

body.heading: When is breathlessness an emergency?
body.body:
Asthma attacks can be life-threatening. During an asthma attack, the NHS says to call 999 if the person does not feel better after using their reliever inhaler as directed, if they feel worse at any time, or if they do not have an inhaler.

COPD symptoms can suddenly get worse in what is called a flare-up. A person unsure what to do can contact their GP or NHS 111 for advice, and 999 is for emergencies. NHS 111 can advise when it is unclear how serious a flare-up is.

A GP can look into new or ongoing breathing problems, because both conditions are diagnosed using symptoms, an examination and lung function tests.

body.heading: What helps people living with either condition?
body.body:
People with asthma are offered regular asthma reviews, where things such as flu vaccination can be discussed. For people with COPD who smoke, the NHS says stopping smoking is the most important step.

The NHS encourages people with COPD to have the yearly flu jab and a one-off pneumococcal vaccination, and for asthma it advises vaccinations such as the flu vaccine because viruses such as flu can make asthma symptoms worse. Flu jabs can be discussed at an asthma review.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: Pulmonary rehabilitation is a programme of exercise and education that can improve how far someone can exercise before becoming breathless. COPD can also come from long-term exposure to harmful fumes or dust, and rarely from a genetic problem that makes the lungs more vulnerable. Having eczema or hay fever, being born prematurely, or growing up around air pollution or cigarette smoke are linked with asthma. Asthma can have normal breathing test results at the time of the test, so one normal result does not always rule it out. NICE says COPD is suspected from symptoms and signs and supported by spirometry, which is also used again if the diagnosis is reconsidered. Flu jabs are given at a GP surgery or a taking-part pharmacy.

references.title: NICE: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in over 16s (NG115)

osteoarthritis-and-rheumatoid-arthritis-.name: Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis
osteoarthritis-and-rheumatoid-arthritis-.headline: Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis: how they differ
osteoarthritis-and-rheumatoid-arthritis-.summary: Osteoarthritis makes joints painful and stiff; rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the joint lining.
keyPoints: Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis in the UK and mostly affects the knees, hips and small joints of the hands.
Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the lining of the joints.
Rheumatoid arthritis usually affects joints on both sides of the body and brings long morning stiffness, as well as tiredness.
Osteoarthritis is managed with exercise, weight management and pain relief; rheumatoid arthritis needs medicines that reduce inflammation.
Early assessment matters for rheumatoid arthritis, so a GP appointment is the first step for persistent joint swelling or stiffness.

body.heading: What do the two conditions have in common?
body.body:
Both osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are types of arthritis, and both cause joint pain and stiffness.

They are not. They have different causes, tend to affect different joints and are treated differently.

body.heading: What is osteoarthritis?
body.body:
Osteoarthritis is a condition that makes joints painful and stiff. The NHS says it is the most common type of arthritis in the UK.

The protective cartilage on the ends of the bones gradually breaks down. The NHS lists several things that raise the risk of osteoarthritis, including age, joint injury, extra weight, being female and family history.

It most often causes problems in the knees, hips and small joints of the hands. The NHS says osteoarthritis does not necessarily get any worse over time.

There is no cure for osteoarthritis, but treatment can help with symptoms.

Hot or cold packs can ease osteoarthritis symptoms.

body.heading: What is rheumatoid arthritis?
body.body:
Rheumatoid arthritis is a long-term condition that causes swollen, stiff and painful joints, most often in the hands and feet. It is an autoimmune disease: the immune system attacks the lining of the joints.

The NHS says it usually affects joints on both sides of the body, and that morning stiffness often lasts longer than it does in osteoarthritis. Some people also have tiredness, a fever or weight loss.

The trigger is not clear, but a higher risk is linked with being female, having a family history of the condition and smoking.

Rheumatoid arthritis can also cause firm lumps called rheumatoid nodules under the skin.

body.heading: How are they treated?
body.body:
For osteoarthritis, the NHS recommends regular exercise, keeping to a healthy weight, suitable footwear and aids that reduce strain on the joint. Medicines can be used to relieve the pain of osteoarthritis, and physiotherapists and occupational therapists can provide structured exercise plans and advice on aids.

Surgery, most often a hip or knee replacement, is generally considered when other treatments are not enough.

Rheumatoid arthritis is treated with medicines that slow the disease and reduce inflammation, known as disease-modifying drugs, sometimes alongside biological treatments. Painkillers and steroids can ease symptoms, and physiotherapy and occupational therapy are part of care. There is no cure, but treatment can help to reduce inflammation, relieve pain and prevent or slow joint damage.

body.heading: How are they diagnosed?
body.body:
A GP asks about symptoms and examines the joints. Osteoarthritis can often be diagnosed from the symptoms and an examination.

For suspected rheumatoid arthritis, blood tests that look for inflammation are used, and the site's pages on CRP and ESR explain two of them. Scans such as X-rays may be done to check for joint inflammation and damage.

No single blood test can prove or rule out rheumatoid arthritis, so doctors combine blood tests, scans and an examination.

Osteoarthritis does not usually need X-rays or blood tests, but they may be used to rule out other causes such as rheumatoid arthritis.

If rheumatoid arthritis is suspected, the GP may do blood tests and refer the person to a specialist.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body:
A GP appointment is the usual route for joint pain, swelling or stiffness that does not settle. The NHS emphasises that early diagnosis and treatment of rheumatoid arthritis can help to prevent joint damage.

If the skin around a joint is red or hot, or sore joints come with a high or low temperature, the NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or getting help from NHS 111.

For sore joints with a high or low temperature, or red or hot skin around a joint, the NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111.

references.title: National Rheumatoid Arthritis Society: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and osteoarthritis (OA)

heartburn-acid-reflux-and-gord.name: Heartburn, acid reflux and GORD
heartburn-acid-reflux-and-gord.headline: Heartburn, acid reflux and GORD: what they are and when to see a GP
heartburn-acid-reflux-and-gord.summary: Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest from acid reflux; when it keeps happening it is called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD).
keyPoints: Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest caused by stomach acid travelling up towards the throat.
When reflux keeps happening it is called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD.
Lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines are the usual first steps, and a pharmacist can advise on options.
Difficulty swallowing, unintentional weight loss or frequent vomiting need prompt advice from a GP or NHS 111.
A GP can prescribe acid-reducing medicine and arrange tests if symptoms continue.

body.heading: What is heartburn, and how does it relate to GORD?
body.body:
Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest. NHS sources describe it as caused by stomach acid travelling up towards the throat, which is known as acid reflux.

If it keeps happening, the condition is called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD.

body.heading: What are the symptoms?
body.body:
The main symptoms of acid reflux are heartburn and an unpleasant sour taste in the mouth caused by stomach acid. Some people also have a hoarse voice, bad breath, bloating or feeling sick.

Symptoms tend to get worse after eating, when lying down or when bending over.

body.heading: What can bring it on?
body.body:
NHS sources list several contributors: certain foods and drinks, being overweight, smoking, stress or anxiety, having a hiatus hernia, and pregnancy.

Some medicines, including anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen, can also play a part.

Heartburn can also come with bad breath.

body.heading: What helps?
body.body:
Lifestyle changes are usually the first step. NHS advice includes eating smaller, more frequent meals, avoiding foods that trigger symptoms, and not eating within a few hours of going to bed. Not smoking is also advised.

Antacids and alginates, which are available from pharmacies, can ease symptoms, and a pharmacist can talk through the options.

Antacids and alginates are not meant to be taken regularly for long periods, so a pharmacist can advise on them.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body:
A GP appointment is the usual route if lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines do not help, or if heartburn happens most days.

Some symptoms need prompt attention, by contacting the GP or NHS 111. NHS sources list difficulty swallowing, unintentional weight loss, food getting stuck in the throat and frequent vomiting as reasons to contact a GP or NHS 111.

Chest pain can also be a sign of a heart problem. The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not ease, especially with sweating, feeling sick, light-headedness or breathlessness, as it may be a heart attack.

Food getting stuck in the throat is another reason to see a GP.

Vomiting blood, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds, needs emergency medical care.

Severe chest pain can be mistaken for heart-related pain, so treat sudden severe chest pain as an emergency and call 999.

body.heading: What can a GP offer?
body.body:
A GP may prescribe a proton pump inhibitor, a medicine that reduces the amount of acid the stomach makes. A GP may prescribe a proton pump inhibitor for a short time, and some people need a long-term prescription, and the NHS advises anyone whose symptoms continue or return to go back to the GP.

If symptoms continue despite treatment, a GP may refer someone for a gastroscopy, a test to look at the lining of the food pipe.

Surgery to strengthen the valve at the bottom of the food pipe exists but is not usually needed.

Long-lasting reflux can sometimes inflame or ulcerate the food pipe.

references.title: Cambridge University Hospitals: Dietary and lifestyle advice for adults with GORD

uti-and-cystitis-what-they-are.name: UTI and cystitis: what they are
uti-and-cystitis-what-they-are.headline: Urinary tract infection and cystitis: symptoms, treatment and when to get help
uti-and-cystitis-what-they-are.summary: A urinary tract infection (UTI) can affect the bladder, urethra or kidneys; cystitis is a UTI of the bladder, and antibiotics are not always needed.
keyPoints: A urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection anywhere in the urinary system, and cystitis is a UTI in the bladder.
Common symptoms are pain or burning when passing urine, needing to go more often, and cloudy urine.
Fever, pain in the back or side below the ribs, or blood in the urine can point to a more serious infection.
Antibiotics can treat UTIs, but the NHS says they are not always needed and many cases can be eased at home.
Urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP is advised for symptoms such as blood in the urine, back pain or a high temperature.

body.heading: What is the difference between a UTI and cystitis?
body.body: A urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection in any part of the urinary system, which includes the kidneys, the tubes that carry urine, the bladder and the urethra. Cystitis is the name for an infection of the bladder.

body.heading: What are the symptoms?
body.body:
The NHS lists burning or pain when passing urine, needing to pass urine more often (including at night), and cloudy urine. Cystitis can also bring lower tummy pain.

A kidney infection is more serious. Symptoms that point towards it include a high temperature, pain in the back or side under the ribs, feeling shivery or unwell, and blood in the urine.

In older people, a kidney infection may cause confusion.

A UTI can also cause blood in the urine, a fever, or feeling hot, cold and shivery.

body.heading: What causes a UTI?
body.body:
UTIs happen when bacteria, usually from the gut, get into the urinary tract. Pregnancy, using spermicide with contraception and not drinking enough fluids are among the things the NHS links with a higher chance of getting one.

People who use a urinary catheter, or who have a weakened immune system, are also at higher risk.

UTIs are more common in women, because the urethra is shorter and sits close to the anus.

body.heading: How is a UTI treated?
body.body:
The NHS says antibiotics are not always needed, and many cases can be eased at home. The NHS says paracetamol and drinking plenty of fluids can ease symptoms, and NHS guidance says there is no evidence that cranberry products help ease symptoms once an infection has started.

A pharmacist can advise on treatment and whether a GP is needed, and a GP may prescribe a short course of antibiotics.

Most kidney infections need prompt treatment with antibiotics, and some people, such as those who are pregnant or have a long-term health condition, may be treated in hospital.

body.heading: When should someone get medical help?
body.body:
The NHS advises contacting a GP or NHS 111 the same day for blood in the urine, pain in the back or side, a very high or low temperature, vomiting, or not having passed urine all day. The same applies to anyone who is pregnant, uses a catheter or has a weakened immune system.

The NHS advises seeing a GP if urinary symptoms have not improved after a few days, or if UTIs keep coming back.

Confusion, drowsiness or difficulty speaking can be a sign of a serious infection, and the route is 999 or A&E.

A very low temperature, feeling or being sick, or not having passed urine all day are also reasons to contact a GP or NHS 111 urgently.

The NHS says confusion, drowsiness or difficulty speaking is a reason to call 999 or go to A&E, with someone else driving rather than the person themselves.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: Some GPs suggest waiting a couple of days before giving antibiotics for a UTI. The NHS suggests avoiding drinks that can irritate the bladder, such as coffee, alcohol and fruit juice. For kidney infections, painkillers like ibuprofen are not usually recommended, so ask a pharmacist or GP what is safe. If UTIs keep coming back, the NHS advises seeing a GP.

migraine-and-tension-headache-compared.name: Migraine and tension headache compared
migraine-and-tension-headache-compared.headline: Migraine and tension-type headache compared: features, treatment and warning signs
migraine-and-tension-headache-compared.summary: Tension headache is usually a dull, tight pressure on both sides of the head, while migraine often throbs and brings nausea or sensitivity to light.
keyPoints: Tension-type headache usually causes a pressing or tightening pain on both sides of the head, with mild to moderate severity.
Migraine is often a throbbing pain that can be moderate to severe, with nausea, vomiting and sensitivity to light and sound.
Some people have an aura before a migraine, and attacks last longer than a typical tension headache.
Painkillers help both, but frequent use of painkillers can itself cause headaches.
A sudden, extremely painful headache, or a headache with loss of vision, confusion or drowsiness, or a rash that does not fade under a glass, needs 999 or A&E.

body.heading: What does a tension headache feel like?
body.body:
Tension-type headache typically causes a dull, pressing or tight-band pain felt on both sides of the head. An NHS-linked self-care leaflet describes tension-type headache as mild to moderate and not made worse by ordinary daily activity.

The NHS says tension headaches last at least 30 minutes and can last for several days. MedlinePlus says tension headaches usually do not cause nausea or vomiting.

The NHS says tension headaches can be eased with painkillers and activities that help with relaxing.

body.heading: What does a migraine feel like?
body.body:
An NHS-linked self-care leaflet describes migraine as usually moderate to severe, on one or both sides of the head, and it can be made worse by ordinary daily activity. Nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light and sound are common.

Attacks typically last for hours, and some people have an aura, a set of temporary symptoms such as visual disturbance, before the headache starts.

Early warning symptoms, such as feeling very tired, can start hours or even a day or two before the head pain.

Aura can include seeing zigzag lines or flashing lights, numbness, dizziness or difficulty speaking.

body.heading: How are they treated?
body.body:
For tension-type headache, NICE advises considering aspirin, paracetamol or an NSAID for the acute treatment, and the NHS mentions activities that help with relaxing. NICE says treatment to help prevent the underlying headache may be offered alongside stopping the medicines that are causing medication-overuse headache.

The NHS migraine page advises taking painkillers as soon as the headache starts. For the acute treatment of migraine, NICE advises offering an oral triptan together with an NSAID, or an oral triptan together with paracetamol.

Taking painkillers or triptans too often can cause medication-overuse headache, which NICE says is treated by stopping the medicines, with advice from a healthcare professional.

body.heading: When is a headache an emergency?
body.body:
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a sudden and extremely painful headache, a headache after a head injury, loss of vision, confusion or drowsiness, a seizure, new numbness or weakness, or a rash that does not fade under a glass.

These signs can mean a serious condition, and getting help promptly matters.

Headaches with vomiting, or vision or eye problems, can need an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111.

Migraine that is new in pregnancy or soon after having a baby is something to speak to a healthcare professional about promptly.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP if headaches happen several times a week or are severe, or if painkillers and relaxing activities do not help.

The site's page on headache sets out causes and warning signs in more detail.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: NHS migraine treatments include painkillers, medicines called triptans, and medicines that help with feeling or being sick. NICE says medication-overuse headache is treated by stopping the painkillers or triptans causing it, with support from a healthcare professional, and headaches may get worse before they improve. A throbbing pain at the front or on one side of the head, or feeling sick or finding light or noise painful, can point to migraine rather than a tension headache.

references.title: Source: nice.org.uk treatment for medication overuse headache

kidney-stones-symptoms-and-treatment.name: Kidney stones: symptoms and treatment
kidney-stones-symptoms-and-treatment.headline: Kidney stones: symptoms, how they are diagnosed and how they are treated
kidney-stones-symptoms-and-treatment.summary: Kidney stones form when chemicals in urine build up; small ones may cause no symptoms, while larger ones can cause severe pain, and some may need a procedure.
keyPoints: Kidney stones form when chemicals from urine build up in the kidneys, and small stones may cause no symptoms.
Larger stones can cause severe pain that comes and goes, sometimes with nausea or blood in the urine.
A GP can often diagnose kidney stones from symptoms and history, with urine and blood tests and sometimes a scan.
Most stones can be treated at home with medicines and plenty of fluids; larger stones may need to be broken up or removed.
Severe pain, a high temperature or feeling hot, cold or shivery needs urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP.

body.heading: What are kidney stones?
body.body:
Kidney stones are hard lumps that form in the kidneys. The NHS says they are caused by chemicals from urine building up in the kidneys.

Small stones often cause no symptoms and may pass unnoticed.

body.heading: What symptoms can they cause?
body.body:
Larger stones can cause severe pain. It can come and go in waves.

Other symptoms can include nausea or vomiting, blood in the urine, sweating, a high temperature and a urine infection.

body.heading: What causes them?
body.body:
The NHS says kidney stones can be caused by dehydration, by some medicines, and by some medical conditions. Not drinking enough water raises the chance of getting one.

Other things that raise the risk include a diet high in protein and low in fibre, being inactive or bed-bound, repeated kidney or urine infections, and a close family member who has had stones.

body.heading: How are kidney stones diagnosed?
body.body:
A GP can usually diagnose kidney stones from the symptoms and medical history. Urine and blood tests may be used.

If the pain is severe, the NHS says the person may be referred to hospital for a scan. If a scan is needed, the NHS says adults have a CT scan, while pregnant women and children under 16 have an ultrasound scan.

body.heading: How are they treated?
body.body:
Most kidney stones can be treated at home. The NHS says this usually means painkillers, anti-sickness medicine, medicines that help a stone pass, and drinking plenty of water.

Larger stones may need to be broken up or removed. One option is shockwave lithotripsy, where shock waves are aimed at the stone to break it up. Other procedures use a thin scope to reach the stone.

body.heading: When should someone get urgent help?
body.body:
The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111 for anyone with kidney stone symptoms who is in severe pain, or has a high temperature, or feels hot, cold or shivery.

A high temperature can be a sign of infection, so it needs prompt advice from a GP or NHS 111. Hospital leaflets advise A&E for anyone who cannot pass urine, and 999 in an emergency.

Hospital leaflets also advise A&E when pain is not controlled by painkillers.

Signs of infection with a stone can include a high temperature, burning when passing urine, and feeling tired or unwell.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: Shockwave lithotripsy can be uncomfortable, so painkillers are usually given first, and more than one session may be needed. In ureteroscopy, a thin telescope is passed through the urethra and bladder into the ureter, and it is done under general anaesthetic.

references.title: NIDDK: Symptoms and causes of kidney stones
Source: guysandstthomas.nhs.uk kidney stone pain renal colic

high-blood-pressure-what-happens-next.name: High blood pressure: what happens next
high-blood-pressure-what-happens-next.headline: High blood pressure: how it is found, what causes it and what treatment involves
high-blood-pressure-what-happens-next.summary: High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms and is found by measuring it; treatment starts with lifestyle changes and may include medicine.
keyPoints: High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, and the only way to know is to have it measured.
In most people no single cause is found; age, family history, ethnicity and lifestyle all play a part.
Readings taken at home or by a 24-hour monitor can be used alongside clinic readings to confirm the diagnosis.
Lifestyle changes are the first step, and a GP may prescribe medicine if blood pressure is very high or stays high.
The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not go away, or chest pain with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness, as it could be a heart attack.

body.heading: What does a blood pressure reading mean?
body.body:
Blood pressure is the force of blood against the walls of the arteries. A reading gives two numbers: the pressure when the heart beats and the pressure between beats. The site's page on blood pressure measurement explains how they are taken.

Doctors use different thresholds for readings taken in a clinic and for readings taken at home when deciding whether blood pressure is high.

body.heading: Does high blood pressure cause symptoms?
body.body:
Usually not. The NHS says high blood pressure often has no symptoms, so many people do not know they have it, and the only way to find out is to have it measured. Rarely it can cause headaches, blurred vision or chest pain.

Over time, the NHS says, untreated high blood pressure raises the chance of problems such as stroke and heart disease.

body.heading: What causes it?
body.body:
For most people there is no obvious cause, which is called essential hypertension, and it can run in families. In a small number of people there is an underlying cause, such as a kidney or adrenal gland condition.

The NHS says risk rises with age, with Black African or Black Caribbean ethnicity, and with a family history. Smoking, drinking too much alcohol, being overweight and not being active are also linked.

The NHS advises calling NHS 111 for frequent headaches or blurred vision, chest pain that comes and goes, or other symptoms thought to come from high blood pressure.

body.heading: How is the diagnosis confirmed?
body.body:
A single clinic reading is usually followed by other checks. NICE advises confirming raised clinic readings with home monitoring or with a 24-hour ambulatory monitor, which takes readings through the day.

Some people have higher readings in a clinic than at home, sometimes called the white coat effect, which is one reason these extra checks are used. A GP may also arrange blood and urine tests and an ECG, which checks the heart rhythm.

A reading taken in a clinic is less accurate than home or ambulatory readings and is not enough on its own to diagnose high blood pressure.

body.heading: What does treatment involve?
body.body:
Lifestyle changes come first for many people. The NHS lists cutting down on salt and alcohol, being more physically active, losing weight where needed, and stopping smoking.

A GP will usually prescribe medicine if blood pressure is very high, if the person has a higher risk of heart attack or stroke, or if it stays high after lifestyle changes. Several types are used, including ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers and diuretics, and the choice depends on things such as age and ethnicity.

Some people need to take blood pressure medicine long term, though if blood pressure stays under control for several years it may be possible to cut back or stop treatment.

Most blood pressure medicines are taken as tablets once a day.

Making lifestyle changes early on may mean some people can avoid needing medicine.

Water tablets (diuretics) work by increasing the amount of salt the kidneys remove.

body.heading: When is it an emergency?
body.body:
The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not go away, or chest pain with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness, as it could be a heart attack.

NHS guidance for pharmacy staff says a very high clinic reading together with symptoms such as headache, palpitations, new confusion or chest pain should be referred to A&E, using 999 where necessary.

references.title: British Heart Foundation: High blood pressure
NICE: Hypertension in adults, diagnosis and management (NG136) visual summary

underactive-and-overactive-thyroid-compa.name: Underactive and overactive thyroid
underactive-and-overactive-thyroid-compa.headline: Underactive and overactive thyroid compared: symptoms, causes and treatment
underactive-and-overactive-thyroid-compa.summary: An underactive thyroid does not make enough thyroid hormone, while an overactive thyroid makes too much; the symptoms, causes and treatments differ.
keyPoints: An underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) means the gland does not make enough thyroid hormone; an overactive one (hyperthyroidism) means it makes too much.
Symptoms differ: an underactive thyroid can cause tiredness, feeling cold and weight gain, while an overactive one can cause nervousness, sensitivity to heat, a fast heartbeat and weight loss.
The main cause of an underactive thyroid in the UK is an autoimmune condition called Hashimoto's disease.
Underactive thyroid is usually treated with levothyroxine tablets; overactive thyroid with medicine, radioactive iodine or surgery.
Treatment for an overactive thyroid can lead to an underactive thyroid, so follow-up blood tests matter.

body.heading: What does the thyroid do?
body.body: The thyroid is a gland in the neck that makes hormones which help control the body's energy use. An underactive thyroid does not make enough of these hormones, while an overactive thyroid makes too much.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of an underactive thyroid?
body.body:
The NHS describes an underactive thyroid as a common condition in which the thyroid does not make enough hormone. Common symptoms include tiredness, feeling colder than usual, weight gain, constipation, low mood, and dry skin or hair.

Symptoms may be mild and can develop slowly, so they are not always easy to notice.

Because the symptoms of an underactive thyroid overlap with other conditions, it cannot be diagnosed from symptoms alone.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of an overactive thyroid?
body.body:
The NHS says an overactive thyroid, also called hyperthyroidism, means the thyroid makes too much hormone. Symptoms can include nervousness, anxiety, mood swings, sleep problems, tiredness, sensitivity to heat, and a fast or irregular heartbeat.

Tremors and weight loss can also occur, and it is unlikely that one person would have all of the symptoms.

body.heading: What causes each condition?
body.body:
In the UK, the main cause of an underactive thyroid is Hashimoto's disease, an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the thyroid.

The main cause of an overactive thyroid is Graves' disease, another autoimmune condition. Thyroid nodules can also cause an overactive thyroid, though less commonly.

Other causes of an underactive thyroid include thyroiditis, neck surgery or radiotherapy, treatment for an overactive thyroid, and some medicines.

body.heading: How are they treated?
body.body:
An underactive thyroid is usually treated with levothyroxine tablets, which replace the missing hormone. The NHS says they are usually needed for life, with regular blood tests to check that the treatment is right.

An overactive thyroid can be treated with antithyroid medicine, radioactive iodine or surgery. Beta blockers can help control some of the symptoms in the meantime, but they do not stop the thyroid making too much hormone.

Radioactive iodine often leads to an underactive thyroid that then needs lifelong hormone tablets.

body.heading: How is the thyroid tested, and when should someone get help?
body.body:
Thyroid function is checked with blood tests that measure thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and thyroid hormones. The site's pages on thyroid function tests and TSH explain them, and the laboratory report shows the reference range used.

A GP can examine the neck and arrange blood tests to check how well the thyroid is working. Thyroid storm is a rare, life-threatening flare-up of an overactive thyroid that the NHS calls a medical emergency, so it needs a 999 call.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: Some people feel better soon after starting levothyroxine, while others do not notice a change in symptoms for several months. An overactive thyroid that is not treated or is poorly controlled can lead to eye problems and pregnancy complications as well as thyroid storm. A high TSH with a low thyroid hormone level in the blood could mean an underactive thyroid, while a low TSH with high thyroid hormone levels usually means an overactive thyroid. Radioactive iodine is not suitable for everyone, for example people who are pregnant or breastfeeding, and surgery is usually kept for cases such as a large goitre or when other treatments cannot be used.

sepsis-warning-signs-and-what-to-do.name: Sepsis: warning signs and when to act
sepsis-warning-signs-and-what-to-do.headline: Sepsis: the warning signs in adults and children and when to call 999
sepsis-warning-signs-and-what-to-do.summary: Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to an infection; the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if sepsis is suspected.
keyPoints: Sepsis can be life-threatening and needs urgent hospital treatment; it can follow an infection such as pneumonia, a urinary tract infection or cellulitis.
Signs in adults include confusion or slurred speech, uncontrollable shivering, muscle pain, difficulty breathing and blue, pale or blotchy skin.
Signs in babies and children include fast or difficult breathing, unusual sleepiness, poor feeding, and a rash that does not fade under a glass.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if someone may have sepsis, and not to drive there.
Treatment is in hospital and usually includes antibiotics, oxygen if needed, and fluids into a vein.

body.heading: What is sepsis?
body.body:
Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to an infection. The NHS says it can develop very quickly and needs urgent treatment in hospital.

It can follow an infection such as pneumonia, a urinary tract infection or cellulitis. The exact cause is not always clear.

body.heading: What are the signs in adults?
body.body:
The NHS lists confusion or slurred speech, uncontrollable shivering, muscle pain, difficulty breathing, and blue, pale or blotchy skin. Passing no urine all day, or very little, is another sign.

Not everyone with sepsis has every sign.

A rash that does not fade under a glass is rare in sepsis, but it can be a sign of meningitis, so call 999 or go to A&E.

In adults, a very high or very low temperature can also be a sign.

body.heading: What are the signs in babies and children?
body.body:
For babies and young children, the NHS lists fast or difficult breathing, blue, pale or blotchy skin, being unusually sleepy, and a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it.

In babies and young children, poor feeding can also be a sign.

body.heading: Who is at higher risk?
body.body:
Anyone can get sepsis, but the chance is higher in babies under 12 months and people over 75. It can sometimes occur in people who are otherwise fit and healthy.

People with a weakened immune system, for example from chemotherapy or from taking corticosteroids or other medicines that suppress the immune system, are also at higher risk.

People with diabetes and people who have recently had surgery are also more likely to develop sepsis.

body.heading: When should someone call 999?
body.body:
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if an adult or child shows signs of sepsis, or if there is a worry that it could be sepsis. It advises asking someone to drive, or calling for an ambulance, rather than driving oneself.

For a worry about an infection when sepsis is not suspected, the NHS says to call NHS 111 or contact the GP. When it is unclear whether it could be sepsis, the NHS says it is still better to call 999.

body.heading: How is sepsis treated, and what happens afterwards?
body.body:
Sepsis is treated in hospital. Treatment usually includes antibiotics, oxygen if needed, and fluids given into a vein. Some people need intensive care.

Recovery can take a long time, and some people take months or longer to feel back to normal. Some people have longer-lasting problems after sepsis, such as tiredness and changes in mood, which is sometimes called post-sepsis syndrome.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: Sometimes surgery is needed to remove the source of infection. Post-sepsis syndrome can also cause problems with memory or concentration, and support such as physiotherapy or counselling may help.

references.title: North East Ambulance Service: Identifying sepsis
Source: nhs.uk who can get it
